questions.q: What does SCD Type 2 do that distinguishes it from SCD Type 1?
options: It preserves history by closing out the old row and inserting a new version, instead of overwriting the value in place
It deletes old rows entirely once an attribute changes
It stores only the current version, identical to SCD1
It requires no surrogate key at all
questions.explain: SCD2's defining behavior is keeping every historical version by expiring the old row and inserting a new one, rather than overwriting in place like SCD1.

questions.q: In the SCD2 table shape, why can the natural key (customer_id) appear in multiple rows while the surrogate key does not repeat?
options: Each row represents one historical version of the customer, so the surrogate key identifies a version, while the natural key identifies the customer across all versions
The natural key is randomly duplicated by Snowflake for performance reasons
Surrogate keys are not allowed to be unique in Snowflake
This only happens due to a data quality bug and should never occur
questions.explain: SCD2 stores one row per version of a customer, so the natural key legitimately repeats across versions while the surrogate key must be unique per version.

questions.q: Why can't a single MERGE statement fully implement SCD Type 2?
options: SCD2 needs to close out an old row while also inserting a new one for the same source row — a third behavior MERGE's WHEN MATCHED / WHEN NOT MATCHED clauses don't provide
MERGE cannot update any column in Snowflake
MERGE cannot reference a staging table as its source
Snowflake does not support the MERGE statement at all
questions.explain: MERGE's two clauses (update matched, insert unmatched) cover SCD1's needs but not SCD2's requirement to both expire an old row and insert a new one for the same changed record, which is why real code splits this into two statements.

questions.q: What does step 1 of the two-step SCD2 pattern do?
options: An UPDATE that sets the expiry_date and flips is_current to FALSE for rows whose tracked attributes changed
An INSERT that adds brand-new customer rows only
A DELETE that removes all historical rows permanently
A CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE that rebuilds the entire dimension from scratch
questions.explain: Step 1 closes out changed rows by setting their expiry_date and marking is_current FALSE, which must happen before step 2 inserts the new versions.

questions.q: Why must step 1 (closing out changed rows) run before step 2 (inserting new versions)?
options: Step 2's anti-join looks for a current row that no longer matches the source, which depends on is_current already being updated by step 1
Snowflake enforces statement ordering automatically and will error if reversed
Step 2 physically cannot run unless step 1's table lock is released
There is no dependency between the two steps; the order doesn't matter
questions.explain: Step 2 identifies rows needing a new version partly by checking for a current row that has stopped matching the source — a check that only works correctly after step 1 has already flipped is_current for changed rows.
